title: The berth *is* the itinerary.
subtitle: Why a smaller ship reaches places a large one can only look at.

text: A port you tender into is a port you can lose to weather.
sub: Moderate swell or wind is enough to suspend tender operations. The ship sits anchored in sight of the town and nobody goes ashore.

points.label: Quay length
points.value: A cruise berth is a finite piece of concrete. The longest ships get sent to anchor.

points.label: Water depth
points.value: Draught rules out some historic harbours entirely, regardless of how new the ship is.

points.label: Who booked first
points.value: Berths are allocated. Two large ships on the same day means one of them anchors.

points.label: Sea state
points.value: Tendering stops for swell and wind long before the sailing itself is at any risk.

title: Three coastlines where this decides the week

items.head: Greek island calls
items.body: Several Cyclades harbours take small ships alongside and send larger ones to anchor offshore.

items.head: The Norwegian fjords
items.body: Small quays in genuinely small villages. Berth length, not ambition, decides who ties up.

items.head: Expedition coastlines
items.body: No quay at all. Here the question is the ship's boats and ice class, not its dining rooms.

text: I read the port list before I read the deck plan.
sub: A summer sailing with four tender calls is a different purchase from the same route docked alongside — and it is usually priced as though it isn't.

title: Send this to your travelling companion
body: Or send me the itinerary you're considering and I'll mark which calls dock and which tender.
